Dupilumab in patients with prurigo nodularis: two randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trials. Nat Med. 2023;29:1180–90." href="/article/10.1186/s12916-026-04952-3#ref-CR27" id="ref-link-section-d302106207e1217">27</a>], underscoring the potential of the therapeutic strategy of anti-IL-4Rα monoclonal antibodies in type 2 inflammatory diseases.</p><p>SHR-1819 is a novel monoclonal antibody that specifically targets human IL-4Rα. Preclinical studies have demonstrated that SHR-1819 exhibits high affinity for human and marmoset IL-4Rα and shows promising biological activity in relevant animal models of AD, rhinitis, and asthma (Data on file, Hengrui). Moreover, SHR-1819 has demonstrated similar inhibitory activity and receptor occupancy profiles to dupilumab against hIL-4/hIL-4Rα in vivo (Data on file, Hengrui). In a first-in-human phase 1 trial involving healthy participants, SHR-1819 was well-tolerated, displayed exposure increasing in a dose-proportional manner, and led to modest reductions in inflammatory biomarkers such as thymus and activation-regulated chemokine/CC chemokine ligand 17 (TARC/CCL17) and immunoglobulin E (IgE) [<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 28" title="Li N, Shakib S, Qian W, Yao X, Li P, Nip TK, et al. Safety, pharmacokinetics, and pharmacodynamics of anti-IL-4Ralpha antibody SHR-1819 in healthy subjects: A randomized, controlled phase I study. Clin Transl Sci. 2024;17:e13763." href="/article/10.1186/s12916-026-04952-3#ref-CR28" id="ref-link-section-d302106207e1223">28</a>]. In this context, we conducted this phase 2 study to investigate the efficacy, safety, pharmacokinetics, and pharmacodynamics of SHR-1819 in patients with moderate-to-severe AD.</p></div></div></section><section data-title="Methods"><div class="c-article-section" id="Sec2-section"><h2 class="c-article-section__title js-section-title js-c-reading-companion-sections-item" id="Sec2">Methods</h2><div class="c-article-section__content" id="Sec2-content"><h3 class="c-article__sub-heading" id="Sec3">Study design and patients</h3><p>This multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 2 trial was conducted in 22 centers in China (ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT05549947).</p><p>Patients aged 18–75 years and had been diagnosed with AD in accordance with the 2014 American Academy of Dermatology guidelines for a minimum of one year prior to screening were enrolled [<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 29" title="Eichenfield LF, Tom WL, Chamlin SL, Feldman SR, Hanifin JM, Simpson EL, et al. Guidelines of care for the management of atopic dermatitis: Sect.  1. Diagnosis and assessment of atopic dermatitis. J Am Acad Dermatol. 2014;70:338–51." href="/article/10.1186/s12916-026-04952-3#ref-CR29" id="ref-link-section-d302106207e1241">29</a>]. Eligible patients were required to have moderate-to-severe AD, as indicated by an Eczema Area and Severity Index (EASI) score of ≥ 16, an Investigator’s Global Assessment (IGA) score of ≥ 3, and a Body Surface Area (BSA) involvement of ≥ 10%. Moreover, patients should have an average of the daily Peak Pruritus Numerical Rating Scale (PP-NRS) score of ≥ 4 over the 7 days preceding randomization and meet at least one of following criteria: suboptimal response to moderate or higher potency topical corticosteroids, prior use of systemic therapy (such as systemic corticosteroids, immunosuppressants, or Janus kinase inhibitors) regardless of treatment response, or ineligibility for topical therapy. Key exclusion criteria are provided in the supplementary methods.</p><p>The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and the Good Clinical Practice Guideline. Protocol received approval from the institutional review board or independent ethics committee of each study center. All participants provided written informed consent before enrollment.</p><h3 class="c-article__sub-heading" id="Sec4">Procedures</h3><p>Patients were randomly assigned (1:1:1:1) to receive SHR-1819 at 300 mg every 2 weeks (Q2W), 600 mg Q2W, 600 mg every 4 weeks (Q4W), or placebo for 16 weeks. A 600 mg initial loading dose was used in the 300 mg Q2W group to expedite the attainment of target concentration levels and accelerate the onset of drug efficacy. This study employed a stratified block randomization method with a block size of 8, stratified by disease severity (moderate [IGA = 3] vs. severe [IGA = 4]). Randomization was performed via a centralized randomization system, under which participating sites competitively enrolled subjects. A dedicated randomization specialist generated the random allocation sequence and drug numbering table using SAS software. The centralized randomization system assigned eligible participants to treatment groups, and corresponding investigational products were dispensed according to the randomization results. All study treatments were prepared as visually identical injectable formulations to maintain blinding, thereby ensuring that patients, investigators, and the sponsor were all kept unaware of the treatment assignment. Requirements for concomitant medications and rescue treatments are provided in the supplementary methods.</p><h3 class="c-article__sub-heading" id="Sec5">Outcomes and assessments</h3><p>The primary endpoint was the proportion of patients achieving ≥ 75% reduction from baseline in EASI score (EASI-75) at week 16. Secondary efficacy endpoints, also assessed at week 16, included the proportion of patients with an IGA score of 0 or 1 (on a 0–4 scale) and a reduction of ≥ 2 points from baseline; the proportion of patients with a reduction of ≥ 2 points in IGA score from baseline; the proportion of patients achieving EASI-90 (EASI score reduction of ≥ 90% from baseline); the proportion of patients achieving EASI-50 (EASI score reduction of ≥ 50% from baseline); the proportion of patients with a reduction of ≥ 4 points from baseline in weekly average of the daily PP-NRS score; as well as the absolute and percentage changes from baseline in EASI score, Scoring Atopic Dermatitis (SCORAD) score, BSA affected by AD, and Dermatology Life Quality Index (DLQI) score. Other secondary endpoints were safety; pharmacokinetics (PK); pharmacodynamics (PD; including TARC/CCL17, IgE, and eotaxin-3 levels and their percentage change from baseline); and immunogenicity.</p><p>Adverse events (AEs) were classified according to the Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities, version 26.0.</p><p>The serum concentration of SHR-1819, TARC/CCL17, and eotaxin-3 levels were quantified using an established enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay method at Shanghai TriApex Biotechnology Co., Ltd. IgE concentrations were measured using the Atellica IM Total IgE assay at the ACL laboratory in the CMAX clinical facility. Anti-drug antibodies (ADAs) were analyzed using electrochemiluminescence at Shanghai TriApex Biotechnology Co., Ltd.</p><h3 class="c-article__sub-heading" id="Sec6">Statistical analysis</h3><p>Assuming an EASI-75 rate at week 16 of 15% in the placebo group and maximum 50% among the three SHR-1819 groups, 37 participants per group (148 in total) could provide the study with 85% power to detect the difference between SHR-1819 and placebo, with a two-sided significance level of 0.05 and an anticipated dropout rate of 15% per group.</p><p>For the primary endpoint, the proportions of patients achieving EASI-75 at week 16 were calculated, with 95% confidence intervals (CI) estimated using the Wilson method. Between-group differences in the proportions and their 95% CIs were estimated using the stratified Mantel-Haenszel method. The stratified Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel method was utilized to compare each dose of SHR-1819 with placebo in the proportion of patients achieving EASI-75 at week 16, and to report the two-sided p-value. When participants discontinued the study treatment, a treatment strategy was adopted (i.e. the data collected in subsequent follow-up visits were included in analysis). When participants received rescue medication, a composite strategy was employed (i.e. the participant was considered as not achieving EASI-75 at week 16). The missing data were imputed using the non-responder imputation (NRI) method (i.e. the participant was considered as not achieving EASI-75 at week 16).</p><p>The same methods as those for the primary endpoint were applied to analyze dichotomous secondary endpoints at week 16. For continuous endpoints at week 16, a mixed-effects model repeated measures (MMRM) analysis was conducted using the restricted estimation maximum likelihood approach. In the MMRM model, baseline scores were used as covariates, with random stratification factors, treatment group, visit, and the interaction between treatment group and visit as fixed effects. The covariance matrix could be either unstructured or compound symmetry as alternative. Intercurrent events were not considered for all secondary endpoints. The missing data for dichotomous secondary endpoints were imputed using the NRI method, while continuous endpoints were handled by the MMRM model.</p><p>All p values are nominal, presented for descriptive and exploratory purposes, and were not adjusted for multiple comparisons. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize baseline characteristics, safety data, PK, PD, and ADA results. Statistical analyses were primarily conducted using SAS version 9.4 or above. See Additional file <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="supplementary material anchor" href="/article/10.1186/s12916-026-04952-3#MOESM1">1</a> for statistical analysis plan.</p></div></div></section><section data-title="Results"><div class="c-article-section" id="Sec7-section"><h2 class="c-article-section__title js-section-title js-c-reading-companion-sections-item" id="Sec7">Results</h2><div class="c-article-section__content" id="Sec7-content"><h3 class="c-article__sub-heading" id="Sec8">Patients</h3><p>From October 26, 2022, to May 26, 2023, 192 patients were screened and 158 eligible patients were randomly assigned. A total of 157 patients received the assigned treatment, with 39, 40, 41, and 37 patients in the SHR-1819 300 mg Q2W, 600 mg Q2W, 600 mg Q4W, and placebo groups, respectively (Fig. <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="figure anchor" href="/article/10.1186/s12916-026-04952-3#Fig1">1</a>). As of database lock (November 23, 2023), 145 patients completed their assigned treatment.</p><div class="c-article-section__figure js-c-reading-companion-figures-item" data-test="figure" data-container-section="figure" id="figure-1" data-title="Fig. 1"><figure><figcaption><b id="Fig1" class="c-article-section__figure-caption" data-test="figure-caption-text">Fig. 1</b></figcaption><div class="c-article-section__figure-content"><div class="c-article-section__figure-item"><picture class="c-article-section__figure-picture"><img aria-describedby="figure-1-desc" src="//media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1186%2Fs12916-026-04952-3/MediaObjects/12916_2026_4952_Fig1_HTML.png" alt="Fig. 1" loading="lazy" width="685" height="304"></picture><div class="c-article-section__figure-link"><a class="c-article__pill-button" data-test="article-link" data-track="click" data-track-label="button" data-track-action="view figure" href="/article/10.1186/s12916-026-04952-3/figures/1" data-track-dest="link:Figure1 Full size image" aria-label="Full size image figure 1" rel="nofollow"><span>Full size image</span><svg width="16" height="16" focusable="false" role="img" aria-hidden="true" class="u-icon"><use xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="#icon-eds-i-chevron-right-small"></use></svg></a></div></div><div class="c-article-section__figure-description" data-test="bottom-caption" id="figure-1-desc"><p>Patient disposition. Q2W, every 2 weeks; Q4W, every 4 weeks</p></div></div></figure></div><p>The demographics and clinical characterization at baseline were well-balanced across groups (Table <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="table anchor" href="/article/10.1186/s12916-026-04952-3#Tab1">1</a>). In the SHR-1819 and placebo groups, 60.0% (72/120) and 62.2% (23/37) of patients had AD lasting ≥ 5 years, respectively.</p><div class="c-article-table" data-test="inline-table" data-container-section="table" id="table-1"><figure><figcaption class="c-article-table__figcaption"><b id="Tab1" data-test="table-caption">Table 1 Demographics and baseline characteristics</b></figcaption><div class="u-text-right u-hide-print"><a class="c-article__pill-button" data-test="table-link" data-track="click" data-track-action="view table" data-track-label="button" rel="nofollow" href="/article/10.1186/s12916-026-04952-3/tables/1" aria-label="Full size table 1"><span>Full size table</span><svg width="16" height="16" focusable="false" role="img" aria-hidden="true" class="u-icon"><use xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="#icon-eds-i-chevron-right-small"></use></svg></a></div></figure></div><p>A total of 17 patients received rescue treatment in this study: 12 during the treatment period and 5 during the safety follow‑up period. Rescue treatment was administered to 4 (10.3%), 1 (2.5%), and 12 (32.4%) patients in the SHR‑1819 300 mg Q2W, 600 mg Q2W, and placebo groups, respectively; no patients in the 600 mg Q4W group received rescue treatment. Among those who received rescue treatment, the majority received topical agents, with only 1 (5.9%) patient in the placebo group requiring systemic therapy.</p><h3 class="c-article__sub-heading" id="Sec10">Efficacy</h3><p>The proportion of patients achieving EASI-75 at week 16 in all three SHR-1819 groups (300 mg Q2W: 69.2% [95% CI: 53.6–81.4]; 600 mg Q2W: 75.0% [95% CI: 59.8–85.8]; 600 mg Q4W: 85.4% [95% CI: 71.6–93.1]) was numerically higher than that in the placebo group (37.8% [95% CI: 24.1–53.9]), with differences of 31.6% (95% CI: 10.3–53.0; nominal <i>p</i> = 0.006), 37.0% (95% CI: 16.3–57.6; nominal <i>p</i> = 0.001), and 47.4% (95% CI: 28.3–66.4; nominal <i>p</i> < 0.001), respectively (Fig. <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="figure anchor" href="/article/10.1186/s12916-026-04952-3#Fig2">2</a>A). The 600 mg Q4W group exhibited the highest EASI-75 response rate among the three SHR-1819 groups at week 16 (Fig. <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="figure anchor" href="/article/10.1186/s12916-026-04952-3#Fig2">2</a>B). Subgroup analysis demonstrated that a trend favoring SHR-1819 over placebo in EASI‑75 response rate was observed across most prespecified subgroups, with nominal <i>p</i> < 0.05 in multiple subgroups for each dose regimen (Additional file 2: Figure S<a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="supplementary material anchor" href="/article/10.1186/s12916-026-04952-3#MOESM2">1</a>). </p><div class="c-article-section__figure js-c-reading-companion-figures-item" data-test="figure" data-container-section="figure" Proportion of patients achieving EASI-50, EASI-75, and EASI-90 at week 16. <b>B</b> Proportion of patients achieving EASI-75 over time. All p values are nominal. EASI, Eczema Area and Severity Index; EASI-50, ≥ 50% reduction from baseline in EASI score; EASI-75, ≥ 75% reduction from baseline in EASI score; EASI-90, ≥ 90% reduction from baseline in EASI score; Q2W, every 2 weeks; Q4W, every 4 weeks</p></div></div></figure></div><p>The LS Mean (SE) percentage change from baseline in EASI at week 16 was −83.14% (3.806), −83.79% (3.697), and −90.18% (3.643) in the SHR-1819 300 mg Q2W, 600 mg Q2W, and 600 mg Q4W groups, respectively, greater compared with the placebo group (−58.61% [3.966]; Additional file 2: Table S<a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="supplementary material anchor" href="/article/10.1186/s12916-026-04952-3#MOESM2">1</a>).</p><p>The percentage of patients in the three SHR-1819 dose groups who achieved an IGA score of 0 or 1 and a reduction of ≥ 2 at week 16 from baseline was higher compared with the placebo group (53.8%, 50.0%, and 65.9% at 300 mg Q2W, 600 mg Q2W, and 600 mg Q4W vs. 16.2%; nominal <i>p</i> = 0.001, = 0.002, and < 0.001, respectively), and the highest proportion was observed in the 600 mg Q4W group (Fig. <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="figure anchor" href="/article/10.1186/s12916-026-04952-3#Fig3">3</a>A and B). Similarly, a greater number of patients in the SHR-1819 groups achieved an IGA score reduction of ≥ 2 at week 16 from baseline compared with the placebo group (66.7%, 62.5%, and 82.9% vs. 37.8%; nominal <i>p</i> = 0.010, = 0.031, and < 0.001; Fig. <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="figure anchor" href="/article/10.1186/s12916-026-04952-3#Fig3">3</a>A).</p><div class="c-article-section__figure js-c-reading-companion-figures-item" data-test="figure" data-container-section="figure" id="figure-3" data-title="Fig. 3"><figure><figcaption><b id="Fig3" class="c-article-section__figure-caption" data-test="figure-caption-text">Fig. 3</b></figcaption><div class="c-article-section__figure-content"><div class="c-article-section__figure-item"><picture class="c-article-section__figure-picture"><source type="image/webp" srcset="//media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1186%2Fs12916-026-04952-3/MediaObjects/12916_2026_4952_Fig3_HTML.png?as=webp"><img aria-describedby="figure-3-desc" src="//media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1186%2Fs12916-026-04952-3/MediaObjects/12916_2026_4952_Fig3_HTML.png" alt="Fig. 3" loading="lazy" width="685" height="1078"></picture><div class="c-article-section__figure-link"><a class="c-article__pill-button" data-test="article-link" data-track="click" data-track-label="button" data-track-action="view figure" href="/article/10.1186/s12916-026-04952-3/figures/3" data-track-dest="link:Figure3 Full size image" aria-label="Full size image figure 3" rel="nofollow"><span>Full size image</span><svg width="16" height="16" focusable="false" role="img" aria-hidden="true" class="u-icon"><use xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="#icon-eds-i-chevron-right-small"></use></svg></a></div></div><div class="c-article-section__figure-description" data-test="bottom-caption" id="figure-3-desc"><p>Efficacy results of IGA and PP-NRS score. <b>A</b> Reductions in IGA and PP-NRS score at week 16. <b>B</b> Proportion of patients achieving IGA score of 0 or 1 and a reduction of ≥ 2 over time. <b>C</b> Percentage change in weekly average of the daily PP-NRS. All p values are nominal. IGA, Investigator’s Global Assessment; PP-NRS, Peak Pruritus Numerical Rating Scale; Q2W, every 2 weeks; Q4W, every 4 weeks</p></div></div></figure></div><p>The proportions of patients achieving an EASI-90 response at week 16 were also higher in the SHR-1819 groups than that in the placebo group (53.8%, 57.5%, and 63.4% vs. 16.2%; <i>p</i> < 0.001 for each comparison; Fig. <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="figure anchor" href="/article/10.1186/s12916-026-04952-3#Fig2">2</a>A). Additionally, a greater proportion of patients in the SHR-1819 groups achieved an EASI-50 response compared with the placebo group (86.4%, 92.5%, 97.6% vs. 54.1%; nominal <i>p</i> = 0.004, < 0.001, and < 0.001; Fig. <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="figure anchor" href="/article/10.1186/s12916-026-04952-3#Fig2">2</a>A).</p><p>Treatment with SHR-1819 also led to a higher percentage of patients achieving a reduction of ≥ 4 points in weekly average of the daily PP-NRS score from baseline at week 16 compared with placebo (41.0%, 47.5%, and 43.9% vs. 16.2%; nominal <i>p</i> = 0.017, 0.004, and 0.007; Fig. <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="figure anchor" href="/article/10.1186/s12916-026-04952-3#Fig3">3</a>A and C).</p><p>Furthermore, all three doses of SHR-1819 resulted in a reduction at week 16 from baseline in the SCORAD index, BSA affected by AD, and DLQI score compared with placebo (Additional file 2: Table S<a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="supplementary material anchor" href="/article/10.1186/s12916-026-04952-3#MOESM2">1</a>).</p><h3 class="c-article__sub-heading" id="Sec12">Safety</h3><p>AEs were reported in 105 (87.5%) of 120 patients treated with SHR-1819 and 30 (81.1%) of 37 patients with placebo (Table <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="table anchor" href="/article/10.1186/s12916-026-04952-3#Tab2">2</a>). The majority were mild or moderate in severity (83.3% with SHR-1819 and 73.0% with placebo), while severe AEs were reported in 4.2% and 8.1% of the patients with SHR-1819 and placebo, respectively. Commonly reported AEs in patients receiving SHR-1819 included upper respiratory tract infection (22.5%), injection site reaction (10.8%), COVID-19 (9.2%), hyperlipidemia (9.2%), increased alanine aminotransferase (8.3%), and hyperuricemia (8.3%). Notably, the incidence and severity of AEs did not show an association with higher doses of SHR-1819.</p><div class="c-article-table" data-test="inline-table" data-container-section="table" id="table-2"><figure><figcaption class="c-article-table__figcaption"><b id="Tab2" data-test="table-caption">Table 2 Safety results</b></figcaption><div class="u-text-right u-hide-print"><a class="c-article__pill-button" data-test="table-link" data-track="click" data-track-action="view table" data-track-label="button" rel="nofollow" href="/article/10.1186/s12916-026-04952-3/tables/2" aria-label="Full size table 2"><span>Full size table</span><svg width="16" height="16" focusable="false" role="img" aria-hidden="true" class="u-icon"><use xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="#icon-eds-i-chevron-right-small"></use></svg></a></div></figure></div><p>Treatment-related AEs (TRAEs) occurred in 55 (45.8%) patients in the SHR-1819 groups and 15 (40.5%) patients in the placebo group (Table <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="table anchor" href="/article/10.1186/s12916-026-04952-3#Tab2">2</a>). Injection site reaction (10.8%), increased blood bilirubin (5.8%), conjunctivitis (5.0%), increased blood uric acid (4.2%), and increased alanine aminotransferase (4.2%) were among the most commonly reported TRAEs in the SHR-1819 group. The majority of TRAEs with SHR-1819 treatment were mild in 40 (33.3%) patients and moderate in 14 (11.7%) patients, with only 1 (0.8%) patient experiencing severe TRAE. The incidence and severity of TRAEs were not correlated with the dosage of SHR-1819.</p><p>Treatment interruptions due to AEs were reported in 8 (6.7%) patients in the SHR-1819 group and 2 (5.4%) in the placebo group. Treatment discontinuations resulting from AEs were reported in 1 (0.8%) patient from the SHR-1819 group and 1 (2.7%) from the placebo group. Serious AEs were noted in 7 (5.8%) patients in the SHR-1819 group and 3 (8.1%) in the placebo group (Additional file 2: Table S<a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="supplementary material anchor" href="/article/10.1186/s12916-026-04952-3#MOESM2">2</a>). Among these serious AEs, 2 (1.3%, dermatitis atopic) were considered treatment-related, with 1 (0.8%) in the SHR-1819 group and 1 (2.7%) in the placebo group. One patient from the SHR-1819 Q4W group died due to AE (brain herniation), and this event was not deemed treatment-related.</p><p>Conjunctivitis occurred in 7 patients (5.8%; all in the SHR-1819 group), including 6 treatment-related events (5.0%). Severity distribution comprised 4 mild and 3 moderate events. Complete resolution was observed in 6 patients (85.7%), and no treatment discontinuations were attributed to conjunctivitis. The majority of laboratory abnormalities were mild, with 7 patients of moderate abnormalities; no severe laboratory abnormalities were observed. All were managed without intervention and resolved or recovered completely.</p><h3 class="c-article__sub-heading" id="Sec13">PK</h3><p>A total of 120 patients were included in the PK analysis. The serum concentration of SHR-1819 gradually increased over the treatment period. The serum drug concentration in the 600 mg Q2W group was higher than those in both the 300 mg Q2W and 600 mg Q4W groups (Additional file 2: Figure S<a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="supplementary material anchor" href="/article/10.1186/s12916-026-04952-3#MOESM2">2</a>).</p><h3 class="c-article__sub-heading" id="Sec14">PD</h3><p>PD analysis was conducted on all 157 patients. SHR-1819 produced a notable decrease in IgE levels across all doses. With multiple administration of SHR-1819, the median percentage decrease in IgE concentration from baseline increased steadily, and maintained until the end of the follow-up period (Additional file 2: Figure S<a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="supplementary material anchor" href="/article/10.1186/s12916-026-04952-3#MOESM2">3</a>A). Similarly, the median percentage reduction from baseline in TARC/CCL17 reached a plateau in 2 weeks after SHR-1819 administration and was sustained until approximately 8 weeks after the last dose (Additional file 2: Figure S<a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="supplementary material anchor" href="/article/10.1186/s12916-026-04952-3#MOESM2">3</a>B). The reduction from baseline in serum eotaxin-3 levels was evident in all SHR-1819 groups starting from week 2 of the treatment period, and this reduction was maintained during the first 4 weeks following the last dose (Additional file 2: Figure S<a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="supplementary material anchor" href="/article/10.1186/s12916-026-04952-3#MOESM2">3</a>C). There was no clear indication of a dose-dependent reduction in IgE and eotaxin-3 levels across different doses, whereas 600 mg Q2W SHR-1819 demonstrated a slightly lower reduction in TARC/CCL17. Exposure-response modeling indicated no obvious correlation between baseline PD biomarkers and clinical endpoints.</p><h3 class="c-article__sub-heading" id="Sec15">Immunogenicity</h3><p>ADA positivity was detected in 3 (7.7%), 2 (5.0%), and 4 (9.8%) patients following SHR-1819 at 300 mg Q2W, 600 mg Q2W, and 600 mg Q4W. There was no discernible relationship between the occurrence of ADA positivity and the SHR-1819 dose.</p></div></div></section><section data-title="Discussion"><div class="c-article-section" id="Sec16-section"><h2 class="c-article-section__title js-section-title js-c-reading-companion-sections-item" id="Sec16">Discussion</h2><div class="c-article-section__content" id="Sec16-content"><p>This phase 2 study demonstrated that SHR-1819 is an effective treatment for moderate-to-severe AD. SHR-1819 produced promising improvements in EASI, IGA, PP-NRS, SCORAD index, BSA affected by AD, and DLQI compared with placebo, indicating efficacy in ameliorating disease severity and alleviating symptoms of AD. SHR-1819 was well-tolerated, and the PK and PD profiles were favorable.</p><p>Dupilumab, an anti-IL-4Rα monoclonal antibody, demonstrated promising improvements in EASI response in the SOLO 1 and SOLO 2 trials (EASI-75 rate: 51% and 44%; EASI-90 rate: 36% and 30%; and EASI-50 rate: 69% and 65%, at week 16) [<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 19" title="Simpson EL, Bieber T, Guttman-Yassky E, Beck LA, Blauvelt A, Cork MJ, et al. Two Phase 3 Trials of Dupilumab versus Placebo in Atopic Dermatitis. N Engl J Med. 2016;375:2335–48." href="/article/10.1186/s12916-026-04952-3#ref-CR19" id="ref-link-section-d302106207e3191">19</a>]. In our study, the proportion of patients achieving EASI-75 (69.2%-85.4%), EASI-90 (53.8%-63.4%), and EASI-50 (84.6%-97.6%) responses at week 16 was numerically higher in the SHR-1819 groups compared with placebo, with the 600 mg Q4W group showing the most substantial improvements. Despite cross-trial comparison should be interpreted with caution due to differences in study design and patient populations, our results preliminarily indicated that SHR-1819 could be a promising treatment choice for moderate-to-severe AD.</p><p>The substantial reduction observed in the PP-NRS score further highlights the beneficial effects of SHR-1819 on pruritus, a hallmark symptom of AD that markedly impacts the quality of life of patients. Moreover, reductions in other efficacy endpoints including IGA scores, SCORAD index, BSA affected by AD, and DLQI score underscore the comprehensive efficacy of SHR-1819 in improving multiple aspects of the disease burden.</p><p>The efficacy of SHR-1819 provides a promising new treatment option for patients with moderate-to-severe AD and offers flexibility in choosing either Q2W or Q4W dosing regimens. The ability to achieve substantial clinical improvement with a once-monthly dosing regimen may offer convenience for patients.</p><p>The safety profile of SHR-1819 was generally favorable and aligned with the biologic therapies targeting IL-4Rα [<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 19" title="Simpson EL, Bieber T, Guttman-Yassky E, Beck LA, Blauvelt A, Cork MJ, et al. Two Phase 3 Trials of Dupilumab versus Placebo in Atopic Dermatitis. N Engl J Med. 2016;375:2335–48." href="/article/10.1186/s12916-026-04952-3#ref-CR19" id="ref-link-section-d302106207e3204">19</a>, <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" title="Thaci D, Simpson EL, Beck LA, Bieber T, Blauvelt A, Papp K, et al. Efficacy and safety of dupilumab in adults with moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis inadequately controlled by topical treatments: a randomised, placebo-controlled, dose-ranging phase 2b trial. Lancet. 2016;387:40–52." href="#ref-CR30" id="ref-link-section-d302106207e3207">30</a>,<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" title="Zhao Y, Wu L, Lu Q, Gao X, Zhu X, Yao X, et al. The efficacy and safety of dupilumab in Chinese patients with moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study. Br J Dermatol. 2022;186:633–41." href="#ref-CR31" id="ref-link-section-d302106207e3207_1">31</a>,<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" title="Paller AS, Silverberg JI, Cork MJ, Guttman-Yassky E, Lockshin B, Irvine AD, et al. Efficacy and Safety of Dupilumab in Patients With Erythrodermic Atopic Dermatitis: A Post Hoc Analysis of 6 Randomized Clinical Trials. JAMA Dermatol. 2023;159:255–66." href="#ref-CR32" id="ref-link-section-d302106207e3207_2">32</a>,<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" title="Gooderham MJ, Hong HC, Eshtiaghi P, Papp KA, Dupilumab. A review of its use in the treatment of atopic dermatitis. J Am Acad Dermatol. 2018;78:S28–36." href="#ref-CR33" id="ref-link-section-d302106207e3207_3">33</a>,<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 34" title="Beck LA, Thaci D, Hamilton JD, Graham NM, Bieber T, Rocklin R, et al. Dupilumab treatment in adults with moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis. N Engl J Med. 2014;371:130–9." href="/article/10.1186/s12916-026-04952-3#ref-CR34" id="ref-link-section-d302106207e3210">34</a>], with no new signals identified. The majority of AEs were mild to moderate in severity. Most serious AEs were unrelated to SHR-1819. The single case of death resulted from a car accident-induced brain herniation, ruling out death caused by central nervous system diseases or drug allergies.</p><p>Infection- and infestation-related AEs were all mild to moderate, resolving or improving with symptomatic treatment or without intervention. The most commonly reported AE was upper respiratory tract infection (22.5% with SHR-1819 and 10.8% with placebo), but only 1.7% in the SHR-1819 group and 5.4% in the placebo group were treatment-related. Conjunctivitis occurred only in the SHR-1819 group, affecting all dose groups without a clear dose-response pattern, consistent with the incidence of conjunctivitis reported with dupilumab targeting the same pathway [<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 19" title="Simpson EL, Bieber T, Guttman-Yassky E, Beck LA, Blauvelt A, Cork MJ, et al. Two Phase 3 Trials of Dupilumab versus Placebo in Atopic Dermatitis. N Engl J Med. 2016;375:2335–48." href="/article/10.1186/s12916-026-04952-3#ref-CR19" id="ref-link-section-d302106207e3216">19</a>]. The incidence of injection site reaction was higher in the SHR-1819 group (10.8%) compared with the placebo group (5.4%), consistent with that with dupilumab [<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 34" title="Beck LA, Thaci D, Hamilton JD, Graham NM, Bieber T, Rocklin R, et al. Dupilumab treatment in adults with moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis. N Engl J Med. 2014;371:130–9." href="/article/10.1186/s12916-026-04952-3#ref-CR34" id="ref-link-section-d302106207e3219">34</a>].</p><p>The drug exposure and PD profiles of SHR-1819 observed in our study align with the known mechanisms of action of IL-4Rα inhibitors [<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 35" title="Clot PF, Kamal M, Sun J, Xu C, Kong F, Gu Y, et al. Dupilumab pharmacokinetics in Chinese healthy subjects and patients with atopic dermatitis: Results of two randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled studies. Int Immunopharmacol. 2021;99:107985." href="/article/10.1186/s12916-026-04952-3#ref-CR35" id="ref-link-section-d302106207e3225">35</a>], providing insights into its potential therapeutic effects. The serum concentration of SHR-1819 increased with dose escalation and remained stable with both Q2W and Q4W administration, supporting the potential for sustained therapeutic effects with both dosing regimens. The PD data showed reductions in IgE, TARC/CCL17, and eotaxin-3 levels, which are known to play key roles in the pathophysiology of AD [<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 36" title="Renert-Yuval Y, Thyssen JP, Bissonnette R, Bieber T, Kabashima K, Hijnen D, et al. Biomarkers in atopic dermatitis-a review on behalf of the International Eczema Council. J Allergy Clin Immunol. 2021;147:1174–e11901171." href="/article/10.1186/s12916-026-04952-3#ref-CR36" id="ref-link-section-d302106207e3228">36</a>], and their reduction potentially correlates with clinical improvement. Notably, the magnitude of these PD marker reductions was comparable between the 600 mg Q4W and 600 mg Q2W groups, which demonstrated a plateau in PD effect with the 600 mg Q4W regimen. The numerically higher EASI-75 rates observed in the 600 mg Q4W group compared with the 600 mg Q2W group likely reflect random variability related to the limited sample size of this phase 2 study rather than a meaningful difference in therapeutic effect. Additionally, the incidence of ADA positivity was low.</p><p>Despite the promising results, this study has several limitations. First, the duration of the trial (16 weeks) was relatively short, and longer-term studies are needed to confirm the sustained efficacy and safety profile of SHR-1819. Second, the study did not include direct comparisons with other biologics such as dupilumab, and head-to-head comparative studies with dupilumab would provide valuable insights into the relative benefits and risks of these two monoclonal antibodies. Future research should also focus on investigating the potential of SHR-1819 in combination with other therapies, such as topical treatments or other systemic agents, which could provide insights into optimizing treatment regimens for AD. Last, this study was conducted only in China; therefore, the generalizability of the findings to other ethnic and geographic populations requires confirmation in future global studies.</p></div></div></section><section data-title="Conclusions"><div class="c-article-section" id="Sec17-section"><h2 class="c-article-section__title js-section-title js-c-reading-companion-sections-item" id="Sec17">Conclusions</h2><div class="c-article-section__content" id="Sec17-content"><p>This phase 2 study demonstrates that SHR-1819 is an effective and well-tolerated treatment in Chinese patients with moderate-to-severe AD. The promising improvements in clinical outcomes, combined with favorable safety, PK, and PD profiles, position SHR-1819 as a promising new therapeutic option. Based on our findings, the 300 mg Q2W and 600 mg Q4W dosing regimens were recommended in subsequent phase 3 trials of SHR-1819. Further research is warranted to establish the role of this novel anti-IL-4Rα antibody in the management of AD.</p></div></div></section>

                    <section data-title="Data availability"><div class="c-article-section" id="data-availability-section"><h2 class="c-article-section__title js-section-title js-c-reading-companion-sections-item" id="data-availability">Data availability</h2><div class="c-article-section__content" id="data-availability-content">
              
              <p>The individual patient data generated during this study will be considered for sharing after the product and indication have been approved by major health authorities. Data may be requested 24 months after study completion. Qualified researchers should submit a proposal to the corresponding authors outlining the reasons for requiring the data. The sponsor will provide the data if the proposal is approved, provided that the requestor signs a data-access agreement. Use of data must comply with the requirements of Human Genetics Resources Administration of China and other country or region–specific regulations.</p>
            </div></div></section><section data-title="Abbreviations"><div class="c-article-section" id="abbreviations-section"><h2 class="c-article-section__title js-section-title js-c-reading-companion-sections-item" id="abbreviations">Abbreviations</h2><div class="c-article-section__content" id="abbreviations-content"><dl class="c-abbreviation_list"><dt class="c-abbreviation_list__term u-text-bold u-float-left u-pr-16" style="min-width:50px;"><dfn>AD:</dfn></dt><dd class="c-abbreviation_list__description u-mb-24">

                  </dd><dt class="c-abbreviation_list__term u-text-bold u-float-left u-pr-16" style="min-width:50px;"><dfn>CCL17:</dfn></dt><dd class="c-abbreviation_list__description u-mb-24">

                  </dd><dt class="c-abbreviation_list__term u-text-bold u-float-left u-pr-16" style="min-width:50px;"><dfn>DLQI:</dfn></dt><dd class="c-abbreviation_list__description u-mb-24">

                  </dd><dt class="c-abbreviation_list__term u-text-bold u-float-left u-pr-16" style="min-width:50px;"><dfn>EASI:</dfn></dt><dd class="c-abbreviation_list__description u-mb-24">
                    <p>Eczema Area and Severity Index</p>
                  </dd><dt class="c-abbreviation_list__term u-text-bold u-float-left u-pr-16" style="min-width:50px;"><dfn>IGA:</dfn></dt><dd class="c-abbreviation_list__description u-mb-24">
                    <p>Investigator’s Global Assessment</p>
                  </dd><dt class="c-abbreviation_list__term u-text-bold u-float-left u-pr-16" style="min-width:50px;"><dfn>IgE:</dfn></dt><dd class="c-abbreviation_list__description u-mb-24">
                    <p>immunoglobulin E</p>
                  </dd><dt class="c-abbreviation_list__term u-text-bold u-float-left u-pr-16" style="min-width:50px;"><dfn>IL-4Rα:</dfn></dt><dd class="c-abbreviation_list__description u-mb-24">
                    <p>IL-4 receptor alpha</p>
